passage:
The common law has long treated contractual silence as a problem to be solved by gap-filling rules: where parties fail to specify a term, courts supply one that reasonable contracting parties in like circumstances would have chosen. This approach rests on the assumption that silence is inadvertent—that the parties simply overlooked the contingency in question. The corrective enterprise is therefore restorative: the court reconstructs the bargain the parties would have struck had they thought the matter through.

Yet silence in contracts is not always inadvertent. Parties sometimes leave terms deliberately open, either because negotiating them would be costly relative to the probability of the contingency arising, or because explicit terms would trigger unwanted legal or regulatory consequences. In such cases, judicial gap-filling may distort rather than restore. The court imputes a preference the parties consciously declined to express, substituting its judgment for a deliberate choice. Scholars who recognize this phenomenon have argued that courts should first ask whether silence was inadvertent or deliberate before reaching for a default rule—a step the common law's current doctrinal apparatus is poorly equipped to take.
comparativeBPassage:
A widely held view in contract scholarship holds that default rules—terms courts supply when parties are silent—should mimic what most parties would want. This majoritarian default approach is administratively convenient and minimizes average error across the range of contracting parties. Yet the approach carries a structural blind spot: it treats all silence as equivalent, regardless of its cause.

An alternative framework, sometimes called penalty defaults, proceeds from a different premise. Where parties have information relevant to an efficient term but one side has stronger incentives to withhold it, the court should supply a term that the better-informed party would find burdensome. Facing an unfavorable default, that party has an incentive to disclose its information and negotiate an explicit term. The penalty default thus uses judicial gap-filling not to restore a hypothetical bargain but to correct a strategic information asymmetry. Critics of this framework object that courts cannot reliably identify which party holds the superior information, and that the approach therefore risks imposing costs on parties who were merely silent for innocent reasons rather than strategic ones. Proponents respond that the objection proves too much: the same epistemic difficulty afflicts majoritarian defaults, which also require courts to estimate what parties would have wanted.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following questions is central to both passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Should courts be permitted to supply contractual terms that parties have left unspecified?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whether the cause of contractual silence should influence how courts respond to it?

choices.label: C
choices.text: What administrative burdens do penalty default rules impose on contracting parties?

choices.label: D
choices.text: How can courts distinguish contracts governed by common law from those governed by statute?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whether majoritarian defaults produce more efficient outcomes than negotiated terms?

explanations.correct: Passage A argues courts should distinguish inadvertent from deliberate silence before gap-filling. Passage B argues that all default frameworks treat silence as equivalent and critiques that assumption. Both therefore focus on whether the cause of silence should matter.
explanations.A: Both passages assume gap-filling is permissible in principle; neither debates that threshold question.
explanations.B: Correct. Both passages center on whether the reason for silence—inadvertent versus deliberate or strategic—should shape the court's response.
explanations.C: Administrative burdens are mentioned only briefly in passage B and are not passage A's concern.
explanations.D: Neither passage addresses the distinction between common-law and statutory contract regimes.
explanations.E: Passage A does not compare majoritarian defaults to negotiated terms; this comparison is only implicit in passage B.

questions.questionStem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to disagree over which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Whether courts ever supply terms that contracting parties did not negotiate

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whether the majoritarian default approach is administratively convenient

choices.label: C
choices.text: Whether the reason a contractual term was left unspecified is relevant to proper gap-filling

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whether some parties leave terms deliberately unspecified

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whether courts possess perfect information about contracting parties' preferences

explanations.correct: Passage A explicitly argues that courts should first determine whether silence was inadvertent or deliberate—making cause directly relevant. Passage B's critique of majoritarian defaults notes they treat all silence as equivalent, and while the penalty-default alternative does attend to cause, B presents both views as contested without endorsing passage A's precise prescription. More precisely, the authors would disagree because passage A urges that the cause of silence must be determined before any default is applied, whereas passage B presents the majoritarian framework—which ignores cause—as a live alternative warranting critique but not yet decisively rejected.
explanations.A: Both passages accept that courts routinely supply unspecified terms; neither contests this basic fact.
explanations.B: Passage B explicitly calls majoritarian defaults 'administratively convenient'; passage A does not dispute this characterization.
explanations.C: Correct. Passage A insists cause is decisive; passage B presents frameworks that differ on whether cause matters, reflecting genuine disagreement over its relevance.
explanations.D: Both passages acknowledge that parties sometimes leave terms deliberately unspecified; this is a shared premise.
explanations.E: Both passages implicitly accept that courts have imperfect information; neither claims courts are omniscient.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following is mentioned in passage B but not in passage A as a justification for a particular approach to contractual gap-filling?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Courts should reconstruct the bargain parties would have struck had they addressed the missing term.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Silence in contracts is sometimes the product of deliberate choice rather than oversight.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Supplying a burdensome default term can induce a better-informed party to disclose information.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gap-filling may distort the agreement when courts impute preferences parties chose not to express.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Negotiating certain terms may be too costly relative to the likelihood of the contingency arising.

explanations.correct: Passage B uniquely introduces the penalty-default rationale: a burdensome default induces the better-informed party to disclose information and negotiate an explicit term. Passage A never invokes information-forcing as a justification.
explanations.A: This restores-the-hypothetical-bargain rationale appears in passage A, not exclusively in B.
explanations.B: Both passages acknowledge that some silence is deliberate; this is not unique to B.
explanations.C: Correct. The information-forcing justification for penalty defaults is presented only in passage B.
explanations.D: Passage A explicitly makes this distortion argument in its second paragraph.
explanations.E: Passage A mentions cost-relative-to-probability as a reason parties leave terms open deliberately.

questions.questionStem: It can be inferred from passage A that the author would most likely regard the penalty default framework described in passage B as

choices.label: A
choices.text: an improvement over majoritarian defaults because it at least acknowledges that some silence is strategic

choices.label: B
choices.text: equally problematic as majoritarian defaults because it still does not require courts to determine the cause of silence before applying a rule

choices.label: C
choices.text: preferable to all other default rules because it corrects information asymmetries that courts cannot otherwise address

choices.label: D
choices.text: inapplicable to cases in which contractual silence arises from inadvertence rather than deliberate choice

choices.label: E
choices.text: an unjustified judicial interference with the freedom of parties to structure their agreements as they see fit

explanations.correct: Passage A's central prescription is that courts should first ask whether silence was inadvertent or deliberate before applying any default rule. The penalty default framework described in B applies a burdensome term to strategic silence without requiring that threshold inquiry—it presupposes strategic silence whenever there is an information asymmetry. Under passage A's logic, this omission is as problematic as the majoritarian approach's omission.
explanations.A: Passage A would not view merely acknowledging strategic silence as sufficient; the author insists on a prior determination before any rule is applied.
explanations.B: Correct. Passage A's argument turns on the necessity of the threshold inquiry; penalty defaults skip that step just as majoritarian defaults do.
explanations.C: Passage A does not endorse any particular default framework; it argues for a prior diagnostic step, not for a specific remedy.
explanations.D: While this is technically true of the penalty-default framework, it is not the inference passage A's logic most strongly supports as a criticism.
explanations.E: Passage A does not invoke freedom of contract as a value; its critique is that gap-filling may distort the actual agreement, not that gap-filling is categorically illegitimate.

questions.questionStem: The author of passage A mentions the possibility that explicit terms might "trigger unwanted legal or regulatory consequences" (passage A) primarily in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: illustrate one reason why contractual silence may be a deliberate strategic choice rather than mere inadvertence

choices.label: B
choices.text: argue that courts should defer to regulatory agencies rather than supply default contractual terms

choices.label: C
choices.text: suggest that parties who draft explicit terms are more likely to engage in bad-faith bargaining

choices.label: D
choices.text: demonstrate that the common law's gap-filling apparatus is superior to statutory contract regimes

choices.label: E
choices.text: provide evidence that judicial gap-filling is always preferable to legislatively mandated terms

explanations.correct: The reference to unwanted legal or regulatory consequences appears as one of two examples of why parties might deliberately leave a term unspecified. It functions to substantiate the passage's claim that silence is not always inadvertent—a premise needed for the author's critique of automatic gap-filling.
explanations.A: Correct. The example supports the broader point that deliberate silence exists, which is the pivot on which passage A's argument turns.
explanations.B: Passage A says nothing about deferring to regulatory agencies; the regulatory reference is purely illustrative.
explanations.C: The passage does not connect explicit terms to bad faith; it connects deliberate silence to regulatory incentives.
explanations.D: Passage A does not compare common law to statutory regimes; the regulatory point is about parties' incentives, not comparative legal systems.
explanations.E: Passage A does not endorse judicial gap-filling as universally preferable; its argument is precisely that gap-filling can go wrong.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Passage A identifies a flaw in existing legal doctrine, and passage B describes two frameworks that address that flaw, evaluating each.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Passage A advocates for a specific default rule, and passage B defends a competing default rule against passage A's criticisms.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Passage A presents a historical account of gap-filling doctrine, and passage B updates that account with recent developments.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passage A introduces a theoretical puzzle, and passage B resolves it by endorsing the penalty default framework.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passage A identifies a conceptual problem in how courts treat contractual silence, and passage B surveys scholarly frameworks that engage the same problem without fully resolving it.

explanations.correct: Passage A diagnoses the problem—courts do not distinguish inadvertent from deliberate silence—and notes that current doctrine lacks tools to make that distinction. Passage B surveys two scholarly responses (majoritarian defaults and penalty defaults), explains each, and presents a debate between critics and proponents without declaring a winner. The relationship is diagnosis in A, unsettled scholarly engagement in B.
explanations.A: Passage A does not advocate a flaw correction; it identifies the problem and calls for a diagnostic step. Passage B does not definitively evaluate the frameworks—it presents an ongoing debate.
explanations.B: Passage A does not advocate any specific default rule; it argues for a prior inquiry. Passage B does not respond to passage A's text.
explanations.C: Passage A is not a historical account; it is an analytical critique of current doctrine.
explanations.D: Passage B does not resolve the puzzle or endorse penalty defaults; it presents both sides of the penalty-default debate.
explanations.E: Correct. A diagnoses a conceptual problem; B surveys frameworks that engage it but leave the debate open.

questions.questionStem: The author of passage B would be most likely to make which one of the following criticisms of the reform proposed in passage A?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The proposal incorrectly assumes that courts are ever justified in supplying terms to contracts that parties have left silent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The proposal replaces one doctrinal framework that ignores the cause of silence with another that faces the same epistemic difficulty in identifying cause.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The proposal is redundant because the majoritarian default approach already accounts for deliberate contractual silence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The proposal overlooks the fact that penalty defaults are more efficient than either inadvertent-silence or deliberate-silence defaults.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The proposal imposes costs on contracting parties by requiring them to litigate the reasons for their silence.

explanations.correct: Passage B's proponents of penalty defaults respond to critics by noting that the epistemic objection—courts cannot reliably identify which party holds superior information—'proves too much' because majoritarian defaults also require courts to estimate what parties would have wanted. By the same logic, passage A's proposal requires courts to determine whether silence was inadvertent or deliberate, which is equally an epistemic challenge courts may be unable to meet. Passage B's author would most likely raise this parallel epistemic difficulty against passage A.
explanations.A: Passage B does not contest the legitimacy of gap-filling in principle; it debates which approach to gap-filling is best.
explanations.B: Correct. Passage B's recurring theme is that epistemic limitations afflict all default frameworks equally; the same objection applies to passage A's diagnostic step.
explanations.C: Passage B explicitly states that majoritarian defaults treat all silence as equivalent, ignoring its cause—so B would not say the majoritarian approach already accounts for deliberate silence.
explanations.D: Passage B does not rank penalty defaults as most efficient; it presents the penalty-default debate neutrally.
explanations.E: Passage B does not raise litigation costs as a critique; its objections are epistemic and structural.
